Parse each 13-digit string (without hyphens) into digits d0 … d12.
Let k be the unknown odd-position weight (2–9) and suppose the swapped pair is at adjacent indices i and i+1 (with 3 ≤ i ≤ 10, so the checksum column 12 and the first three columns are untouched).

With the digits in their erroneous order, define:
A = Σ even-index digits (0,2,4,6,8,10)
B = Σ odd-index digits (1,3,5,7,9,11)
Δ = d_{i+1} − d_i (difference between the two digits that were swapped)

After restoring the swap, the corrected weighted sum S′ of the first 12 digits becomes
• if i is even:  S′ = A + Δ + k(B − Δ)
• if i is odd:   S′ = A − Δ + k(B + Δ)

The checksum condition is  (S′ + d12) ≡ 0 (mod 10)  ⇒  α + kβ ≡ 0 (mod 10) where
α = A ± Δ + d12,   β = B ∓ Δ   (signs depend on the parity of i).
For every code the same pair (k,i) must satisfy this congruence.

Testing all k ∈ {2,…,9} and i ∈ {3,…,10} gives the following results:
• i = 3,4,5,6,7,8,10 – no single k satisfies all ten congruences.
• i = 9 – the congruence system reduces for the ten codes to
   2k ≡ 4, 8k ≡ 6, 3k ≡ 1, 1k ≡ 7, 6k ≡ 2, 6k ≡ 2, 3k ≡ 1, 7k ≡ 9, 4k ≡ 6, 7k ≡ 9  (mod 10)
   whose unique common solution in 2 ≤ k ≤ 9 is k = 7.

Therefore the only weight–index pair that corrects all ten numbers is weight 7 with the swap between columns 9 and 10 (smaller index 9).
Let k be the unknown odd-index weight and let i be the smaller of the two transposed indices (0-based).

For each 13-digit string, write the weighted sum of the first 12 digits as
    S =  (sum of even-index digits) + k·(sum of odd-index digits).
The checksum condition is (S + c) ≡ 0 (mod 10), where c is the last digit.

If columns i and i+1 have been swapped, the change in the weighted sum for one code is
    Δ = (w_i − w_{i+1})(d_{i+1} − d_i)
          = ±(k−1)(d_{i+1} − d_i),
with the sign “+” when i is odd, “−” when i is even.
After swapping we need Δ ≡ −e (mod 10) where e = (S + c) (mod 10) for the uncorrected code.

Thus, for every code we must have
   (k−1)(d_{i+1} − d_i) ≡ {  e (mod 10)  if i even
                           −e (mod 10)  if i odd }.
Checking all i from 3 to 10 and k from 2 to 9, the only pair that satisfies this congruence simultaneously for all ten strings is
   k = 7,   i = 9.
Verifying: swapping digits at positions 9 and 10 and using weights 1 and 7 makes each corrected 13-digit number pass the checksum test.

Therefore the unique feasible solution is weight 7 with transposed columns 9 and 10, so the required pair is 7, 9.
